strengths: The paper asks a clear, well-motivated question (why does feature-map KD work for CNNs but fail for ViTs?) and structures the investigation around a concrete 'paradox' (globally low-rank teacher yet hard to distill), which makes the narrative easy to follow.

The two-view analysis (global SVD + token-level spectral energy) is an interesting attempt to disentangle global subspace dimensionality from per-token channel utilization, and is applied consistently across six architectures (Table 1, Figures 1-8) with quantile-based ranks that support the low-rank claim.

Experiments use a paired, single-factor design on ImageNet-1K with a standard 300-epoch DeiT recipe, and the ablations (head type, projector width, loss weight, multiple teachers, standalone-without-teacher) are well chosen; the standalone result (Table 7) is a nice touch that tests the architectural-bottleneck claim independent of distillation.

The proposed remedies are minimal and practical, and the finding that retaining a projector at inference plus last-block widening reactivates simple MSE feature KD (+2.3 to +3.4 points over baseline) is a useful empirical result with actionable design guidance.
Writing and figure presentation are generally clear; training details (hyperparameters, batch size, hardware) are reported at a level that aids reproduction.
weaknesses: The central diagnostic (SEP) lacks validity controls. Applying a 1D DFT along the channel dimension is questionable because ViT channels have no meaningful ordering: the metric is not permutation-invariant, and a flat, near-diagonal cumulative energy curve is exactly what one expects for a generic high-dimensional random vector. Without null comparisons (e.g., shuffled channels, random features, or CNN features), the 'high per-token bandwidth' finding may reflect generic spectral behavior rather than a learned encoding law; the suspiciously identical b_80%≈0.80 / b_90%≈0.90 across all architectures (Table 8) reinforces this concern. The causal claim that this 'encoding mismatch' explains KD failure therefore remains speculative.

The 'paradox' framing is partly manufactured: a globally low-rank representation with dense per-token coordinates is the expected situation (tokens in a low-dim subspace need not be sparse in any basis), so the two observations are not obviously contradictory, and the paper does not establish that resolving this geometric tension is actually what makes distillation work.

A critical baseline is missing: Table 2 reports unmodified DeiT-Tiny with feature-only SpectralKD (75.07) but never unmodified DeiT-Tiny + SoftKD (logits) alone. Without this control it is impossible to isolate how much of the headline gain (e.g., Strategy 1 SoftKD 77.23) comes from the architectural modification versus simply applying logit distillation, which weakens the paper's central attribution.

The incremental benefit attributable to feature KD after the modification is modest (e.g., SoftKD 77.23 vs SoftKD+MSE 77.50 for Strategy 1, a +0.27 difference), and no seed variance or confidence intervals are reported anywhere despite many conclusions resting on differences of 0.1-0.5 points (e.g., Table 4, where the claimed 384-dim sweet spot is within noise of 320-dim).

Generality and cost accounting are limited: the student is always DeiT-Tiny; parameter/FLOP counts for the widened final block (Strategy 2) are never reported despite 'compact ViT' framing (a 384-wide final block is substantially heavier than 192); and intermediate-layer distillation, where most feature-KD methods operate, is not analyzed - only the last layer.

Novelty is moderate: retaining a linear projector at inference is close to well-known practice (FitNets-style projection; the authors themselves cite [32] on the role of projectors), and SpectralKD [34] already performs spectral analysis of ViTs for distillation; the paper should more sharply delineate its contribution relative to these works. No code release is mentioned, further limiting reproducibility of the ImageNet-scale claims.

strengths: The paper asks a clear and well-motivated question: why does CNN-style feature-map KD underperform on ViTs, and it attempts an answer through a diagnostic analysis (layer-wise SVD plus token-level spectral energy) rather than only proposing a new loss.

The proposed remedies are refreshingly simple and honest: a post-hoc linear projector retained at inference, and widening only the student's last block. The experiments are accompanied by a paired, one-factor-at-a-time design and reasonable ablations (head type, projector width, loss weight, multiple teachers), which makes the empirical deltas easy to interpret.

The observation that architectural modifications improve the student even without any teacher (Table 7) is a nice sanity check supporting the claim that the last-layer bottleneck is architectural rather than a distillation artifact.
The writing is clear and the analysis pipeline (SVD histograms, SEP curves, appendix per-model plots) is documented in enough detail to be broadly reproducible from the text.
weaknesses: The headline 'globally low-rank' claim is overstated and partially an artifact. The SVD is computed per image on an N x D token-by-channel matrix (N ~ 197 for 224x224/16), so the rank is capped at ~197 regardless of the 384 channel width. Requiring 121 of a maximum ~197 components for 99% energy (Figure 1) is not dramatically low-rank, yet the paper compares only against D=384 and never mentions the token-count ceiling. Similarly, the strikingly low Swin stage-3 ranks (mean ~10) are trivially explained by the tiny token count at that stage (7x7). The central 'low-rank yet hard to distill paradox' rests on this flawed framing.

The SEP analysis lacks validity controls and may be close to a tautology. A 1D DFT along the channel dimension depends on an arbitrary channel ordering, and dense basis vectors of a low-rank subspace will naturally spread per-token energy across most coordinates. Without control experiments (e.g., SEP of random Gaussian tokens, isotropic features, or CNN features), a nearly diagonal SEP curve (Figure 2, Table 8) cannot be interpreted as a meaningful 'encoding law,' and ViT-Tiny shows the same diagonal curve, so the diagnostic does not actually separate teachers from students.

The causal story connecting the analysis to the remedies is not established. The gains from Strategy 1 could stem from many confounds (extra parameters, a softened loss landscape, a learnable pathway to the head) rather than 'per-token encoding capacity.' No experiment isolates capacity per se, e.g., matching parameter counts, or distilling into the low-rank subspace identified by SVD versus full width. The paper's own ablation (Table 4) shows a 320-dim projector slightly beats the teacher-matched 384-dim standalone, which weakly contradicts the subspace-matching narrative.

Insufficient comparison to the state of the art. The main claim of 'reactivating' feature KD (74.86 -> 78.23 with a CaiT-S24 teacher) is not contextualized against strong published distillation results for DeiT-Tiny-scale students (e.g., ScaleKD, TinyViT, DistillToken, FKD), nor against the closely related projector-focused work the paper itself cites ([32] Miles & Mikolajczyk on the role of the projector, [31] ViTKD, [35] Distillation Dynamics). The delta over cited prior work is not clearly articulated.

Narrow scope and missing costs. Experiments are confined to ImageNet-1K classification with essentially one student (DeiT-Tiny) and 384-dim teachers; Strategy 1's retained projector adds inference-time parameters and latency that are never quantified; there is no limitations discussion, no downstream/transfer evaluation, and no analysis of intermediate-layer distillation, which is where most feature-KD methods operate.

Generality claims are weaker than advertised. Table 6 shows the gains shrink substantially with same-family teachers (e.g., +0.80 to +1.64 with DeiT-Small/DeiT3-Small versus +3.37 with CaiT-S24), yet the abstract and conclusion present the remedy as general.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated and clearly stated question — why feature-map KD works for CNNs but not ViTs — and frames a genuine puzzle: final-layer ViT features are globally low-rank, yet naive linear alignment underperforms.

The two-view diagnostic (layer-wise SVD + token-level SEP) is an interesting analytical lens, and the empirical rank/bandwidth statistics across six architectures (CaiT-S24, DeiT-Small, Swin-Small, ViT-Large/Huge/Tiny) are reported thoroughly, with per-model plots and variance bands in the appendix.

The proposed remedies are directly tied to the diagnosis, and the experiments provide a reasonable causal test of the mismatch hypothesis: with the width mismatch removed (projector retained at inference, or widened last block), vanilla MSE feature KD goes from nearly useless (+0.21) to consistently beneficial (+1.75 to +2.29), and gains hold across three different teachers.

Experimental hygiene is above average: a paired one-factor-at-a-time design, standard DeiT recipe, ablations over head type, projector width, and loss weight, plus a teacher-free control (Tables 2–7) showing the architectural change helps even without distillation.
Writing is clear and the analysis-to-method pipeline is easy to follow; training details (batch size, LR schedule, hardware) are specific enough to support reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central mechanistic claim rests partly on the SEP metric, whose evidential value is questionable. A 1D DFT along the channel dimension has no natural frequency semantics (channels are not ordered), and an almost perfectly diagonal cumulative-energy curve with b80 ≈ 0.8 for every model is close to what any generic, non-sparse vector would produce. The appendix's suspiciously uniform values across all architectures (Table 8) are consistent with the SEP curve being a property of typical real-valued vectors rather than a distinctive ViT 'encoding law'. The paper does not compare against a random-baseline SEP or against CNN features, so the 'high per-token utilization' finding may be less informative than claimed.

Several obvious controls are missing: (a) the framing is CNN-vs-ViT, yet no CNN experiments are included; (b) no distillation between same-width ViT pairs (e.g., CaiT-S24 teacher → 384-dim student) to confirm that feature KD works without any modification once the width mismatch is absent; (c) the SVD analysis suggests projecting the teacher down to its ~121-dim subspace for alignment, which is never tested; (d) only a linear projector is tried, with no nonlinear MLP-projector comparison, despite the projector's role being well studied (Miles & Mikolajczyk, which the paper cites).

Baseline coverage is thin. The comparison set is essentially SoftKD and SpectralKD; recent strong ViT distillation methods (ScaleKD, fine-grained manifold distillation, ViTKD variants) are cited but not compared, making it hard to judge whether the proposed strategies are competitive or merely 'less broken'.

No variance reporting anywhere: single runs, no seeds, no error bars. Several claimed effects are small (standalone gains of +0.55/+0.68; several ablation gaps of ~0.1–0.3 points), so statistical significance is unclear.

The methods themselves are architecturally simple and individually close to known practice (linear feature projector in FitNets-style KD; an inverted-bottleneck-like widened final block). The novelty rests almost entirely on the diagnostic story, so if the SEP interpretation is weak, the methodological contribution is modest.
No explicit limitations section, and no code release is mentioned, which weakens reproducibility of a paper whose contribution is primarily empirical analysis.

strengths: The core empirical diagnosis is well executed and broad: the contrast between per-image SVD effective ranks (e.g., 61/384 dims for 95% energy on CaiT-S24) and dataset-level PCA requirements (302/384 for the same images) is quantified across 14 models spanning supervised, self-supervised, and multimodal training regimes, with full per-model diagnostics in the appendix (Figures 3-15). This is a clear, useful clarification of the per-image vs. dataset-level 'low-rank' conflation (building on Yu & Wu 2023).

The paper is honest that both remedies improve the student even without a teacher (Table 7: +0.55/+0.68), correctly interpreting this as an architectural bottleneck rather than a purely distillation-specific effect, and the limitations/future-work discussion (intermediate layers, adaptive lifting) is reasonable.

Ablations are reasonably thorough for the proposed methods: classifier head type, projector output dimension (including the finding that widening beyond teacher width hurts), and feature-loss weight, plus generality checks with DeiT-Small and DeiT3-Small teachers.

The writing is generally clear and well structured; the paradox framing (per-image compressibility yet dataset-level non-compressibility under a shared projector) is easy to follow, and code/raw data are reportedly provided, aiding reproducibility.

The headline ImageNet-1K results are strong in absolute terms (DeiT-Tiny + CaiT-S24: 74.86% to 78.23%), and the observation that vanilla MSE feature KD becomes reliably beneficial once the interface is widened is an interesting empirical finding.
weaknesses: A critical control is missing: the baseline DeiT-Tiny + SoftKD (logit-only KD) without any architectural change is never reported. Lift+SoftKD (77.23) and WideLast+SoftKD (77.88) are headline numbers, but since Lift/WideLast also add parameters/capacity (WideLast widens the last block from 192 to 384 dims, likely adding ~40% parameters to a 5.7M model; parameter/FLOPs counts are never reported), the gains cannot be cleanly attributed to resolving the 'encoding mismatch' versus simply a slightly larger student plus standard logit distillation. Standalone gains (+0.55/+0.68) suggest a large fraction of the headline improvement may come from SoftKD alone on any model.

The causal story is internally inconsistent: Lift is explicitly a fixed, input-independent mapping and the paper concedes it 'does not resolve dataset-level subspace rotation,' yet it performs nearly as well as WideLast. This undercuts the claimed importance of the subspace-rotation facet of the diagnosis; the analysis-to-remedy link is asserted more than demonstrated (no experiment isolates rotation vs. bandwidth, e.g., by aligning to a random or fixed wide subspace).

The SEP diagnostic is under-justified. Applying a 1D DFT along the channel dimension is semantically arbitrary (channel ordering carries no meaningful structure), and the near-diagonal cumulative energy profile may be close to a generic property of channel-mixed token vectors rather than an 'architecture-invariant encoding law.' The paper does not provide a null-model control (e.g., SEP of permuted-channel or random-feature baselines) to establish that the diagonal profile is a nontrivial finding, and the link from 'high spectral bandwidth' to the failure of a narrow student is loose: if features lie in a low-rank subspace, a linear map from a 192-dim student should in principle reach that subspace regardless of per-token DFT profile.

Novelty of the remedies is modest and positioning against closely related work is thin. 'Lift' is essentially adding an inference-time projector, a well-studied device (the paper itself cites Miles & Mikolajczyk 2024 on projector roles, ScaleKD, VkD, OFA-KD), and none of these strong feature-KD baselines are compared head-to-head under the paper's own setup; the only feature-KD comparison is SpectralKD, which the paper shows is weak in this regime. Without comparisons to ViTKD/ScaleKD/RSD-style methods, the claim that these fixes 'reactivate' feature KD is hard to contextualize.

Generality is limited: the main claims rest on one student (DeiT-Tiny) with CaiT-S24, and gains shrink substantially for DeiT-Small/DeiT3-Small teachers (+0.78 to +1.64 in Table 6). Everything is on ImageNet-1K at 224x224; no transfer tasks, no other domains, and the appendix evidence (Appendix B/C) is diagnostic only, not experimental validation of the mechanism.

The 'encoding mismatch' narrative occasionally overstates: describing a near-linear energy-vs-bandwidth curve as a 'law' and 'spectral universality' is presented strongly relative to the (uncontrolled) evidence, and the paper does not discuss whether the SEP regularity could follow trivially from the whitening-like structure of high-level token features.

strengths: The empirical diagnostics are extensive and consistent: per-image SVD vs. dataset-level PCA comparisons are repeated across ~15 architectures spanning supervised, self-supervised (DINO, MAE, DINOv2), and multimodal (CLIP) pretraining, with full per-model figures and statistics in the appendix (Figures 3-15, Tables 1, 8), supporting reproducibility of the measurements.

The paper is clearly written and carefully distinguishes per-image low rank from dataset-level shared-subspace requirements, explicitly avoiding the common conflation of sample-wise and population-wise compressibility (Section 2.1, 2.4).

The proposed interventions are minimal and well-ablated: ablations cover classifier head type, projector output dimension, and feature loss weight (Tables 3-5), and generality is tested with multiple teachers (Table 6).
The standalone result without distillation (Table 7) is a nice control showing the endpoint-width effect is not purely a distillation artifact.
The training protocol follows the standard DeiT recipe with reasonable detail, and code/raw data are promised in supplementary materials.
weaknesses: The SEP 'encoding law' is under-supported and possibly tautological. A near-diagonal cumulative spectral energy curve (capturing alpha% of energy from alpha% of bins) is approximately the null expectation for a roughly flat spectrum; the paper presents no baseline (e.g., shuffled tokens, random features, alternative representations) against which 'high bandwidth' should be judged. The 'architecture-invariant' universality (Table 8: b_alpha ~ alpha for every model) therefore reads as a restatement of spectral flatness rather than a discovered law.

The DFT along the channel dimension lacks justification: channels have no natural ordering, so the spectral framing is permutation-dependent. If the result survives arbitrary channel permutations, the SEP analysis reduces to a standard participation-ratio/effective-rank statistic of the token vector, stripping the 'spectral' interpretation of content. The paper does not test this.

The causal link between the analysis and the fixes is confounded. Lift + SoftKD alone (no feature KD) achieves 77.23%, so most of the gain comes from adding endpoint capacity plus logit KD, not from 'reactivating' feature-map alignment. The standalone gains (+0.55/+0.68) further suggest a generic architectural effect of extra last-layer capacity, not a specific resolution of the diagnosed mismatch. No experiment isolates the claimed mechanism (e.g., distilling from a teacher whose subspace rotation is artificially controlled).

Baseline comparisons are weak. The paper compares against naive SpectralKD on the plain student but not against strong published compression-distillation methods for DeiT-Tiny (e.g., DKD, ViTKD, ScaleKD, TinyMIM-style recipes), so it is unclear whether 78.23% is competitive or simply the effect of extra parameters in a standard recipe.

The 'anomalies' in the own data are not discussed: MAE models show dataset-PCA required dimension of 1 at 80% energy (Table 1, Figures 11-13), which contradicts the universal subspace-rotation narrative and suggests the diagnostics are sensitive to representation structure the paper does not characterize.

Experimental scope is narrow: a single student (DeiT-Tiny), a single primary teacher (CaiT-S24), one dataset (ImageNet-1K), and the generality experiments use same-width teachers where gains are small (+0.78 to +1.64) and where the width-mismatch premise barely holds.

No seed variance or error bars are reported; several conclusions rest on differences of 0.1-0.3% (e.g., 75.41 vs. 75.54 in Table 7, SpectralKD 76.40 vs. 76.48 across projector dims in Table 4), which are within typical run-to-run variability for ViTs on ImageNet.

The remedies are close to known practice: projector-based alignment (analyzed by Miles & Mikolajczyk, 2024) and last-block capacity adjustments are simple engineering choices; the paper's novelty rests heavily on the SEP diagnostic, which as noted above is the weakest component.

The 'endpoint capacity mismatch' story is asserted rather than quantified: the paper never measures the student's SEP or per-image rank during/after training to show that matching these quantities predicts distillation success, so the diagnosis-to-fix connection remains correlational.

strengths: The central diagnostic finding is clean and well-motivated: the paper cleanly separates per-image low-rank structure (SVD) from dataset-level shared-subspace requirements (PCA), and documents the resulting 'subspace rotation' across a broad set of architectures and training regimes (Table 1, Figures 3-15), which is genuinely illuminating and goes beyond the common 'features are low-rank' folklore.
The two proposed remedies are minimal, well-scoped, and directly tied to the diagnosis; the results are substantial for the primary setting (DeiT-Tiny from CaiT-S24: 74.86% to 77.53%/78.23%).
The standalone (no-teacher) experiments (Table 7) are a nice touch: they support the claim that the last-layer mismatch is an architectural bottleneck rather than a distillation artifact.

Reasonable robustness checks are included: classifier head choice, projector output dimension (including the instructive finding that lifting beyond teacher width hurts), feature-loss weight, and generality across three teachers.

The writing is clear, the paradox framing is engaging, and the training protocol is described in enough detail (recipe, batch size, hardware, epochs) to be largely reproducible, with code and raw diagnostics promised in supplementary materials.
weaknesses: The SEP 'architecture-invariant encoding law' is the weakest analytical link. A cumulative spectral energy curve that is nearly diagonal in normalized coordinates (b_alpha ~ alpha) is precisely what one expects from an approximately flat spectrum, which is also what white/noise-like or arbitrarily permuted channel orderings would produce. The DFT is applied along the channel dimension, which has no canonical ordering, so 'frequency bins' have no natural meaning. The paper does not show what a null/hypothesis-free comparison would look like, so 'high per-token bandwidth' may partly be a trivial property rather than a discovered encoding law.

The causal chain from diagnosis to remedy is asserted more than verified. No experiment directly confirms the mechanism, e.g., measuring whether lifted/widened students achieve higher E_i(d) or better per-token SEP agreement with the teacher, or that failure correlates with measured mismatch. WideLast's claimed advantage (input-dependent subspace realization) is plausible but untested.

Baselines against prior art are incomplete. The comparison set is limited to the unmodified DeiT-Tiny, plain SpectralKD, and internal ablations; there is no head-to-head with established ViT compression KD methods (e.g., DeiT's distillation token under the same schedule, ScaleKD, ViTKD, RSD), so it is unclear whether 78.23% is competitive with or merely restores feature KD relative to the state of the art.

No parameter/FLOPs accounting. Both Lift and WideLast add capacity at the endpoint (WideLast's 384-wide last attention+MLP block roughly quadruples that block's parameters relative to 192-dim), yet no overhead figures are reported and the gains are not normalized against matched-parameter baselines, which matters for a compression paper.

Single-run results without seeds or variance estimates; several ablation deltas are small (e.g., +0.55/+0.68 standalone; head-type differences), and some generality numbers (Table 6) show inconsistent patterns between Lift and WideLast across teachers that are not analyzed.

Method novelty is modest: retaining a wider final projection or widening the final block are natural, near-obvious interventions once the diagnosis is made, and prior work (e.g., Miles & Mikolajczyk on projectors; ScaleKD's learned projectors) has explored endpoint alignment capacity; the paper's contribution rests heavily on the analysis being novel and correct, so the questionable SEP interpretation weakens the overall package.

The analysis covers only the last layer; the paper itself concedes that intermediate-layer mismatch, where most feature KD is actually applied in practice, is unexplored, which limits the practical scope of the 'failure mechanism' claim.
